pos: v. and n. (to pass the night; to give shelter — in Scripture the hinge of hospitality, and the measure of what dwells in a city)
etymology: From Old French logier, to shelter, from loge, a hut or arbour — ultimately from a Germanic root meaning a covering of leaves. The oldest sense is a temporary booth, which is exactly the sense of the Hebrew malon, a night's lodging place on a journey.
biblical_def: Lodge is a traveller's word, and in a world without inns it was the pivot on which the duty of hospitality turned. Ruth makes it a vow: “whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Rut 1:16) — conversion and covenant loyalty expressed as a decision about where to sleep. Abraham's servant asks it at the well as the test of a household: “is there room in thy father's house for us to lodge in?” (Gen 24:23). The Lord Jesus, who said the Son of man had not where to lay his head, kept the practice: after cleansing the temple “he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany; and he lodged there” (Mat 21:17). And Isaiah turns the word into a moral inventory of a city: “How is the faithful city become an harlot! it was full of judgment; righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers” (Isa 1:21) — righteousness had been a resident of Jerusalem, and had moved out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lodge as to set or lay down, to place; to furnish with a temporary habitation; and intransitively, to reside, to rest, to pass the night.
webster_full: LODGE, v.t. To set, lay or deposit for keeping or preservation, for a longer or shorter time.
2. To place; to plant; to infix.
3. To furnish with a temporary habitation, or with an accommodation for a night.
LODGE, v.i. To reside; to dwell; to rest in a place.
2. To rest or dwell for a time, as for a night; as, where lodgest thou?
scriptures: Rut 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
And said, Whose daughter art thou? tell me, I pray thee: is there room in thy father's house for us to lodge in?
And he left them, and went out of the city into Bethany; and he lodged there.
Isa 1:21
How is the faithful city become an harlot! it was full of judgment; righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers.
corruption_summary: Hospitality is reduced to entertaining friends in a presentable house, when the New Testament commands it as a duty toward strangers and makes it a qualification for office.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek word is philoxenia, love of strangers, and its opposite is not a shabby house but a closed one. Scripture commands it plainly — “given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13), “use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9) — and makes it a requirement for elders, who must be “a lover of hospitality” (Tit 1:8). Modern practice has converted it into entertaining, which is a performance for people who already belong and which stalls whenever the house is untidy or the budget is thin. Ruth was a Moabitess with nothing; the servant at the well was an unknown foreigner asking a girl for lodging for ten camels and their men.

Isa 1:21 supplies the sobering measure. A city is described by what lodges in it — righteousness once did, and murderers now do — and the same test can be put to a household or a heart. What has taken up residence? Hospitality matters partly because it is the visible form of the answer: a house where strangers are received is a house where righteousness still has a room. Heb 13:2 adds the incentive Scripture chooses: be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
roots_summary: Old French logier, to shelter; rendering Hebrew lun (H3885), to pass the night, and malon (H4411), a lodging place, and Greek aulizomai (G835), to lodge in the open or in a courtyard.
roots_lines: Hebrew lun (H3885) — to lodge, pass the night; also, in another stem, to murmur — the wilderness generation's nights and their complaining share a root.
Hebrew malon (H4411) — a lodging place on a journey; the inn at which Moses was met by the LORD (Exo 4:24).
Greek aulizomai (G835) — to lodge, spend the night; used of Christ at Bethany (Mat 21:17).
Greek xenizo (G3579) — to receive as a guest, to lodge a stranger; Peter lodged with Simon a tanner (Act 10:6).
Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, the New Testament word for hospitality (Rom 12:13; Heb 13:2).
usage: “Where thou lodgest, I will lodge” — covenant loyalty settled as a question of where to sleep.
“Is there room… for us to lodge in?” — the question that tested a household.
“Righteousness lodged in it” — a city measured by its residents.

pos: v. (to go and bring; in Scripture the errand of hospitality, the prophet's test of a widow, and the wise woman's word for restoring the banished)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon feccan, to bring — probably a variant of fetian, to go and get. English kept the two-part sense the Hebrew also has: fetch is not merely to bring but to go and bring.
biblical_def: Fetch is a servant's verb, and Scripture puts it in some surprising mouths. Abraham uses it of himself at Mamre, running the errand for his own guests: “I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts” (Gen 18:5) — and the morsel turns into a calf, cakes, butter and milk, the pattern of hospitality that promises little and gives much. Elijah uses it as a test of a widow at the end of her resources: “Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink” (1Ki 17:10), the first of three requests that would each cost her more than the last. The Law uses it to protect the poor from a creditor's intrusion: “When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge” (Deu 24:10) — a man's home is not open to his lender. And the wise woman of Tekoa uses it for the restoration of an exile, in the sentence that persuades David about Absalom: “the king doth not fetch home again his banished” (2Sa 14:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fetch as to go and bring; to bring, to go for and produce — and also, to bring back, to recall, and to derive or draw from a source.
webster_full: FETCH, v.t. To go and bring; to go and take from a place, and bring to another.
Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel. 1 Kings xvii.
2. To derive; to draw, as from a source.
3. To bring back; to recall; to bring to any state; as, to fetch a man to life.
4. To reach; to arrive at; to come to; as, the ship fetched the port.
scriptures: Gen 18:5
And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said.

So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, the widow woman was there gathering of sticks: and he called to her, and said, Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.
When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge.

And the woman said, Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God? for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished.
corruption_summary: The Zarephath narrative is turned into a seed-faith parable — give the prophet your last meal and God will multiply your money — which mistakes a famine miracle for a financial method.
corruption_paragraphs: 1Ki 17 is one of the most heavily abused passages in the prosperity repertoire: the widow gives her last handful to the man of God, and the barrel of meal does not waste. Preached as a principle, it becomes a fundraising instrument — sow into this ministry from your poverty and expect return. But the text is a famine narrative in which a Gentile widow is sustained day by day, not enriched; the meal and the oil last exactly as long as the drought and no longer, and her son dies in the next paragraph. Whatever else the chapter teaches, it does not teach that giving is an investment vehicle.

What it does teach is the sovereign extension of mercy beyond Israel, which is precisely how the Lord Jesus used it in the synagogue at Nazareth — many widows were in Israel, and to none of them was Elijah sent, but to Sarepta (Luk 4:25-26) — and the congregation tried to throw Him off a cliff for saying so. Deu 24:10 shows the same God protecting the poor in ordinary law: a creditor may take a pledge but may not walk into a man's house to fetch it, and if the pledge is his cloak it goes back before sundown. That is what care for the poor looks like in Scripture: enforceable limits on the powerful, not a promise of returns to the desperate.
roots_summary: Anglo-Saxon feccan, to go and bring; rendering Hebrew laqach (H3947), to take, and bo (H935) in the causative, to bring.
roots_lines: Anglo-Saxon feccan — to go and bring; the errand and the carrying are both in the word.
Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, fetch, receive; “I will fetch a morsel of bread” (Gen 18:5).
Hebrew bo (H935), hiphil hebi — to cause to come, to bring; “fetch me… a little water” (1Ki 17:10).
Hebrew shub (H7725), hiphil — to bring back; “fetch home again his banished” (2Sa 14:13), the verb of restoration and of repentance alike.
Hebrew abot (H5667) — a pledge given for a loan; the thing the creditor may not enter a house to fetch (Deu 24:10).
usage: “I will fetch a morsel of bread” — and set before them a calf, cakes, butter and milk.
“Fetch me… a little water” — the first of three requests, each costlier than the last.
“Doth not fetch home again his banished” — a wise woman's word for restoration.

pos: n. (that which occupies a man; his employment or affair — in Scripture both the Father's business and the honest labour of one's own hands)
etymology: From busy (Anglo-Saxon bysig) plus -ness: literally the state of being busy, hence the thing that occupies. The commercial narrowing of the word is modern; in 1611 it meant any occupation or matter in hand.
biblical_def: Business in the Authorized Version means whatever a man has in hand, and Scripture speaks well of it. The Lord Jesus uses it of His own vocation at twelve years old, in His first recorded words: “wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?” (Luk 2:49). Paul places diligence in daily work inside a list of spiritual duties without any sense of descending a level: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord” (Rom 12:11) — the three clauses belong together, and a man cannot claim the second while neglecting the first. To the Thessalonians, some of whom had stopped working in expectation of the Lord's return, he writes: “study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you” (1Th 4:11). And Proverbs promises that competence is noticed: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men” (Pro 22:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines business as employment; that which occupies the time and attention; and also as an affair, a matter in hand, or a concern of any kind.
webster_full: BUSINESS, n. Employment; that which occupies the time, attention and labor of men, for the purpose of profit or improvement.
2. Any particular occupation or employment engaged in for a livelihood or gain, as agriculture, trade or a profession.
3. Affair; concern; that which engages the attention.
You have undertaken a business that is above your reach.
4. Serious engagement; important occupation, in distinction from trivial affairs.
scriptures: Luk 2:49
And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
corruption_summary: A sacred-secular divide is imposed on Scripture, so that ministry counts as the Lord's work and ordinary labour does not — and, on the other side, business is baptised as a ministry to excuse whatever it takes to succeed.
corruption_paragraphs: Rom 12:11 does not permit the divide. Paul writes not slothful in business, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord as one breath, and Col 3:23 makes it explicit for the lowest station in the ancient world: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” — addressed to slaves. The Reformation recovered this against the medieval assumption that the monastic life was the higher calling; Luther's doctrine of vocation and Calvin's treatment of the ordinary station both rest on it. A carpenter, a nurse, and a pastor are all in the Lord's work, and only one of them draws a salary from the church.

The corollary corruption is the entrepreneurial gospel that treats a company as a ministry in order to sanctify its ambitions, so that ruthlessness becomes stewardship and self-promotion becomes influence. 1Th 4:11 sets a strikingly unglamorous standard: study to be quiet, do your own business, work with your own hands. Paul's stated reason follows in the next verse — that ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing. Ordinary competent work, done quietly, is a testimony, and it is the one Scripture actually commands.
roots_summary: English busy + -ness; rendering Greek spoude (G4710), diligence, in Rom 12:11, and ta tou patros, “the things of my Father”, in Luk 2:49, and Hebrew melakah (H4399), work or occupation.
roots_lines: Hebrew melakah (H4399) — work, occupation, business; the word for the labour forbidden on the sabbath and for a craftsman's trade.
Greek spoude (G4710) — haste, earnestness, diligence; “not slothful in business” is literally not lagging in diligence.
Greek ta tou patros mou — “the things of my Father” (Luk 2:49); the KJV supplies business, others house; both senses are in the phrase.
Greek ta idia — “your own business” (1Th 4:11); the same construction Paul uses against the busybodies of 2Th 3:11.
Greek periergazomai (G4020) — to be a busybody, literally to work around a thing; the counterfeit of real business.
usage: “About my Father's business” — the Lord's first recorded words, at twelve.
“Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit” — one breath, not two categories.
“Diligent in his business… shall stand before kings” — competence is noticed.

pos: v. (to utter a loud mournful cry; the prophets' command to a people about to be judged, and the sound of the wilderness)
etymology: An imitative word, Middle English houlen, akin to German heulen — the sound is in the syllable. The Hebrew yalal is imitative in exactly the same way, and gives the wailing-word helel and the noun for a wilderness's howling.
biblical_def: Howl is a prophet's imperative, and it is nearly always addressed to people who do not yet think they have anything to howl about. Isaiah opens the burden of Babylon with it: “Howl ye; for the day of the LORD is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty” (Isa 13:6) — the command to mourn is issued before the ruin arrives, which is mercy, since it is a summons to see what is coming while there is time. Joel wakes the comfortable the same way: “Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine” (Joe 1:5). Zephaniah aims it at the commercial quarter of Jerusalem: “Howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the merchant people are cut down; all they that bear silver are cut off” (Zep 1:11). James carries the same prophetic voice into the New Testament without softening it: “Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you” (Jas 5:1). The word also names the sound of a place without people: the “waste howling wilderness” in which the LORD found Jacob (Deu 32:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines howl as to cry as a dog or wolf; to utter a particular kind of loud, protracted and mournful sound — and, of persons, to wail, to lament with a loud cry.
webster_full: HOWL, v.i. To cry as a dog or wolf; to utter a particular kind of loud, protracted and mournful sound.
2. To utter a loud, mournful sound, as a person in distress; to wail.
Howl ye, for the day of the Lord is at hand. Is. xiii.
3. To roar, as a tempest; as, the howling blast.
HOWL, n. The cry of a dog or wolf; a loud, protracted, mournful cry.
scriptures: Isa 13:6
Howl ye; for the day of the LORD is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty.
Jas 5:1
Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.
Joe 1:5
Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth.
He found him in a desert land, and in the waste howling wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.
corruption_summary: The prophetic summons to mourn is edited out of preaching as negative, leaving a pulpit that can comfort the afflicted but can no longer afflict the comfortable.
corruption_paragraphs: A ministry built on encouragement alone has no vocabulary for Isa 13:6 or Jas 5:1, and so it simply stops preaching them. But the command to howl is not cruelty; it is the alarm sounded before the fire reaches the house. Joel calls the drunkards to awake and weep precisely because they are asleep, and the whole book of Joel moves from that summons to “turn ye even to me with all your heart, with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning” (Joe 2:12). Godly sorrow, Paul says, worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of (2Co 7:10). A preaching that cannot produce sorrow cannot produce that repentance either.

Jas 5:1 also refuses the comfortable division that assigns the prophets' economic language to the Old Testament and leaves the New Testament to interior piety. James addresses rich men who have kept back the hire of the labourers by fraud, and says the cries of the reapers have entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. That is not the vocabulary of political economy imported into Scripture; it is Scripture's own. The dictionary rejects the frameworks that make oppression a matter of group identity rather than of sin, and affirms without hesitation what James actually says: God hears defrauded workmen, and the men who defraud them should howl.
roots_summary: Imitative, Middle English houlen; rendering Hebrew yalal (H3213), to howl or wail, and Greek ololuzo (G3649), to howl aloud — itself an imitative word.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalal (H3213) — to howl, wail; an imitative root, the prophets' standard imperative of lament.
Hebrew yelalah (H3215) — a howling, wailing; the noun for the sound itself.
Hebrew yelel (H3214) — a howling; “the waste howling wilderness” of Deu 32:10, a place defined by the cry of its beasts.
Greek ololuzo (G3649) — to howl, shriek; used once in the New Testament, at Jas 5:1, and imitative in Greek as in English.
Isa 14:12 — helel, rendered Lucifer, from the same consonants as the wailing root in one derivation, and from “to shine” in another.
usage: “Howl ye; for the day of the LORD is at hand” — the alarm sounded before the fire arrives.
“Ye rich men, weep and howl” — the prophetic voice, undiminished, in the New Testament.
“The waste howling wilderness” — where the LORD found Jacob and kept him as the apple of His eye.

pos: v. (to remove a covering; in the Law the standing euphemism for sexual sin, and the forbidden act of priestly mourning)
etymology: From un- (reversing) plus cover, Old French covrir, from Latin cooperire. In Scripture the word is the exact opposite of what God did for Adam and Eve, who were covered with coats of skins at the cost of a life.
biblical_def: Uncover is a covenant word with three distinct uses. In Leviticus 18 and 20 it is the fixed legal euphemism for sexual sin, and the chapter opens with the general prohibition: “None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD” (Lev 18:6). What follows is the incest code, and the closing verses ground it in creation and in judgment on the nations that practised otherwise. Second, it is forbidden to the priest in mourning: after the death of Nadab and Abihu, Moses says to Aaron and his surviving sons, “Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die” (Lev 10:6) — the ordinary signs of grief are denied to the man in office, because the priest represents God before the people even in his own bereavement. Third, it is a judicial act: in the trial of jealousy the priest is to “uncover the woman's head” (Num 5:18), an exposure before God in a case no human witness could settle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uncover as to divest of a cover; to remove a covering from; to lay open or expose to view; and also to deprive of clothes, to strip.
webster_full: UNCOVER, v.t. To divest of a cover; to remove any covering from.
2. To deprive of clothes; to strip; to make naked.
3. To take the hat or cap from the head; to bare the head.
4. To lay open; to disclose; to reveal.
Note. To uncover the nakedness, in the Levitical law, is a phrase denoting unlawful commerce of the sexes.
scriptures: Lev 18:6
None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.
Lev 10:6

And Moses said unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar and unto Ithamar, his sons, Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die, and lest wrath come upon all the people: but let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the LORD hath kindled.
Num 5:18

And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD, and uncover the woman's head, and put the offering of memorial in her hands, which is the jealousy offering: and the priest shall have in his hand the bitter water that causeth the curse:
Isa 7:15
Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 18 is set aside as ritual purity law with no moral force, chiefly in order to detach its sexual prohibitions from any claim on the present.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard move in affirming readings of Scripture is to sort the Levitical material into ceremonial rules that lapsed with the temple and moral rules that abide, and then to place chapter 18 in the first pile. The chapter itself blocks this. Its prohibitions are grounded not in Israel's cultic distinctiveness but in what the Canaanites did and why the land vomited them out (Lev 18:24-28) — and the nations were not under the ceremonial law. The New Testament reasons the same way: Paul rebukes the Corinthian church for a case of a man with his father's wife, calls it fornication not named among the Gentiles, and applies the Levitical categories directly (1Co 5:1).

Lev 10:6 addresses a different reader, and a harder one. Aaron has just lost two sons under judgment, and he is forbidden the ordinary signs of grief because he is in office and the office is not his own. The passage does not deny grief — the whole house of Israel is to bewail the burning — but it does say that a man who stands between God and the people bears a restraint that others do not. Every elder and pastor who has had to carry a private sorrow through a public duty has stood in Aaron's place, and the text is a comfort as well as a demand: he stayed at the altar, and God kept him there.
roots_summary: English un- + cover; rendering Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover, remove, and hence to go into exile — one root for nakedness, revelation, and captivity.
roots_lines: Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, reveal, and to be carried away captive; exile is the nation stripped and exposed.
Hebrew galah ervah — “to uncover nakedness”; the standing legal formula for unlawful sexual union in Lev 18 and 20.
Hebrew ervah (H6172) — nakedness, shame, indecency; the noun behind the euphemism.
Hebrew para (H6544) — to let loose, uncover the head; Lev 10:6 and Num 5:18, the loosed hair of mourning and of accusation.
Gen 3:21 — the LORD God made coats of skins and clothed them; the covering God supplies at the cost of a life is the answer to every uncovering.
usage: “To uncover their nakedness” — the Law's fixed euphemism for sexual sin.
“Uncover not your heads” — grief restrained in the man who holds the office.
“Uncover the woman's head” — exposure before God where no witness could settle it.

pos: v. (to carry into effect; in Scripture what God does with judgment and justice, and what He delegates to the magistrate)
etymology: From Latin exsequi — ex- (out) plus sequi (to follow): literally to follow out, to pursue a thing to its conclusion. To execute judgment is not to pronounce it but to carry it through.
biblical_def: Execute in Scripture is almost always paired with judgment, and the pairing is deliberate: a verdict that is never carried out is not justice. God executes it Himself, and He does it for the defenceless: “He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment” (Deu 10:18). He promises to do it through the Messiah: “I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth” (Jer 23:5). He has committed it to the Son: “hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man” (Joh 5:27) — the office belongs to Him precisely as the incarnate one, a man judging men. And He delegates a limited share of it to the civil magistrate: “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). The sword is real, it is not the church's, and it is held on God's commission.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines execute as to perform, to do, to effect; to carry into complete effect; and specially, to inflict a sentence of death, or to carry into effect a judgment of law.
webster_full: EXECUTE, v.t. To perform; to do; to effect; to carry into complete effect; to complete; to finish.
To execute a purpose, a plan or scheme.
2. To inflict; as, to execute judgment or vengeance.
3. To carry into effect the sentence of the law; to put to death.
Note. From the Latin exsequor, ex and sequor, to follow out or pursue to the end.
scriptures: He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment.
Jer 23:5
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
Joh 5:27
And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: Rom 13 is pressed in two opposite directions — into an unconditional obedience that sanctifies any regime, and into an anarchism that denies the magistrate any sword at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The first error reads “the powers that be are ordained of God” as a blank endorsement of whoever holds power, and it has been used to bless tyrannies from the Erastian settlements down to the twentieth century. Paul's own sentence limits the office by describing it: the magistrate is a minister of God for good, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. A ruler who rewards evil and punishes good is not exercising the office but abusing it, and the Reformed political tradition — the Vindiciae contra tyrannos, Knox, Rutherford's Lex Rex — drew the conclusion that the king is under the law. Peter's we ought to obey God rather than men (Act 5:29) sets the boundary.

The second error denies the sword altogether, and it usually arrives by way of the Sermon on the Mount: since the Christian is not to resist evil or return blow for blow, no Christian may bear the sword. But Rom 13 and Mat 5 address different subjects. Mat 5 governs private retaliation; Rom 13 governs the public office, and the same apostle who forbids personal vengeance says God has appointed a revenger to execute it. Deu 10:18 shows why this matters most to the weak: the fatherless and the widow have no power to enforce a verdict of their own, and God's executing of judgment on their behalf, through the magistrate He appoints, is their only protection.
roots_summary: Latin exsequi, to follow out; rendering Hebrew asah (H6213), to do, with mishpat, judgment, and Greek poieo (G4160) with krisis, and ekdikos (G1558), an avenger.
roots_lines: Latin exsequi — ex- out + sequi to follow; to pursue a matter to its conclusion.
Hebrew asah mishpat — literally “to do judgment”; the standing idiom rendered execute judgment (Deu 10:18; Jer 23:5).
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) and tsedaqah (H6666) — judgment and justice or righteousness; the royal pair the Branch will execute in the earth.
Greek krisis (G2920) — judgment, the act of judging; Joh 5:27, given to the Son as Son of man.
Greek ekdikos (G1558) — an avenger, one who carries out justice; the magistrate in Rom 13:4.
usage: “He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow” — a verdict carried through, for those who cannot enforce one.
“A King shall reign… and shall execute judgment and justice” — the Branch of David.
“A revenger to execute wrath” — the magistrate's sword, real and delegated.

pos: n. and v. (a scroll of a book; also to turn over — in Scripture the form the word of God took, and the stone at the sepulchre)
etymology: From Old French rolle, from Latin rotulus, a little wheel — a written sheet wound around a rod. Before the codex, every book was a roll, so roll and book were the same object; English still calls a list a roll for this reason.
biblical_def: Roll is the Authorized Version's word for a scroll, and therefore for the physical form in which God's word came to the prophets. Jeremiah is commanded: “Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah” (Jer 36:2) — and Jehoiakim cuts that roll with a penknife and burns it leaf by leaf, whereupon God commands another with more words added. Ezekiel is handed one: “when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein” (Eze 2:9) — and he is told to eat it before he preaches it. The verb governs two of Scripture's great reversals. At Gilgal the LORD says, “This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you” (Josh 5:9). And at the sepulchre the women ask the question the angel has already answered: “Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?” (Mar 16:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines roll as a writing formed into a cylinder, a scroll or volume; also a register or catalogue; and, as a verb, to turn on an axis, or to move by turning.
webster_full: ROLL, n. The act of rolling, or state of being rolled.
2. A writing formed into a cylinder; a scroll; a volume.
Take thee a roll of a book. Jer. xxxvi.
3. A register; a catalogue or official document; as, the roll of a court.
ROLL, v.t. To turn on an axis; to move by turning; as, to roll a stone.
scriptures: Jer 36:2

Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah, even unto this day.
Eze 2:9
And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein;
Josh 5:9
This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you.
Mar 16:3
And they said among themselves, Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?
corruption_summary: Jer 36 is read as evidence that the prophetic books are layered, edited compilations, when the chapter is Scripture's own account of how inspired dictation survives an attack on it.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship treats Jeremiah 36 as a window onto the editorial process behind the book — a first edition, a second, later expansions — and uses it to license a general theory of prophetic literature as accumulated tradition. The chapter is telling a different story. God dictates; Baruch writes at Jeremiah's mouth; the king destroys the roll; and God commands a second roll with “all the former words… and there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jer 36:32). The point is that the word of God cannot be burned out of existence — it comes back longer — and the process from first roll to second is under the same divine dictation as the first.

The same chapter is a standing rebuke to a subtler habit. Jehoiakim did not argue with the roll; he cut it and burned it in pieces, and “they were not afraid, nor rent their garments” (Jer 36:24). Contrast Josiah his father, who rent his clothes at the reading of the book. A man may dispose of Scripture without ever denying a word of it, simply by keeping it away from the fire in his hearth and the fear in his heart. And Josh 5:9 and Mar 16:3 supply the counterweight: what is rolled away in Scripture — the reproach of Egypt, the stone at the tomb — is always rolled away by God before His people arrive to worry about it.
roots_summary: Latin rotulus, a little wheel; rendering Hebrew megillah (H4039), a roll or scroll, from galal, to roll, and Greek apokulio (G617), to roll away.
roots_lines: Hebrew galal (H1556) — to roll; the root of Gilgal, the place named for the rolling away of the reproach of Egypt (Josh 5:9).
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, scroll; the word for the volume Jeremiah dictated and Ezekiel ate, and the name of the five festival Megilloth.
Hebrew taar hassopher — the scribe's penknife, with which Jehoiakim cut the roll (Jer 36:23).
Greek biblion (G975) — a scroll, book; “the volume of the book” of Heb 10:7, quoting Psa 40:7.
Greek apokulio (G617) — to roll away; the stone at the sepulchre (Mar 16:3-4), and in every Gospel already rolled away before the women arrive.
usage: “Take thee a roll of a book” — dictation that a penknife could not destroy.
“A roll of a book was therein” — and Ezekiel was told to eat it before preaching it.
“Who shall roll us away the stone?” — a question already answered before it was asked.

pos: n. (a territory under an imperial governor; in Scripture the administrative unit of Persia and Rome, and the setting of Esther, Daniel, and Paul)
etymology: From Latin provincia, a territory outside Italy under Roman administration; the derivation is disputed, but the sense is fixed — a conquered land governed from elsewhere. The modern figurative sense (that is not my province) grows from the idea of an assigned jurisdiction.
biblical_def: Province is the vocabulary of empire, and it appears wherever God's people are living under one. Esther opens with the extent of it: Ahasuerus “reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces” (Est 1:1) — a scale that makes the decree against the Jews unstoppable by any ordinary means, which is exactly the book's point. Daniel is promoted within it: “Daniel requested of the king, and he set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, over the affairs of the province of Babylon” (Dan 2:49) — believers administering a pagan empire faithfully, and refusing it at exactly one point. And Paul's legal standing turns on it: “when the governor had read the letter, he asked of what province he was. And when he understood that he was of Cilicia” (Act 23:34) — jurisdiction, the question that would eventually carry him to Caesar. The word quietly frames a large part of the Bible's political theology: God's people are usually a minority under someone else's administration, and Scripture teaches them to serve well, obey where they can, and refuse where they must.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines province as a country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; a country governed by a deputy or governor — and, figuratively, the proper office or business of a person.
webster_full: PROVINCE, n. A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; usually a country at some distance from the kingdom or state to which it belongs.
2. The proper office or business of a person.
It is the province of the judge to determine the law.
3. A region of country; a tract; a district.
Note. Among the Romans, a province was a country without the limits of Italy, subject to a governor sent from Rome.
scriptures: Est 1:1
Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, (this is Ahasuerus which reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces:)
Dan 2:49
Then Daniel requested of the king, and he set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, over the affairs of the province of Babylon: but Daniel sat in the gate of the king.
And when the governor had read the letter, he asked of what province he was. And when he understood that he was of Cilicia;
Jer 23:5
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
corruption_summary: Esther and Daniel are treated as historical romance set in a vaguely remembered Persia, and the exiles' pattern of faithful public service is replaced by either withdrawal or assimilation.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical treatment of Esther and Daniel as second-century fiction rests largely on claimed historical inaccuracies that the archaeology has repeatedly narrowed — Belshazzar, once cited as Daniel's decisive error, turned up in the Nabonidus material as co-regent, which also explains why Daniel is offered the third place in the kingdom. The dictionary holds a sixth-century Daniel and a historical Esther, and notes that the administrative detail these books contain, down to the hundred and twenty-seven provinces and the workings of the royal post, is the sort of thing a later romancer gets wrong and a contemporary gets right.

The pattern they set is the one modern believers most need and most often abandon in one of two directions. Daniel and his friends administered Babylon's province competently for decades — they were not a resistance movement and they were not chaplains — and they refused at exactly the points where obedience to the empire meant disobedience to God: the king's meat, the image on the plain, the thirty-day decree. Withdrawal from public life forfeits the good those men did; assimilation forfeits the refusal. Jer 29:7 gives the working rule for the exile: seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away, and pray unto the LORD for it.
roots_summary: Latin provincia; rendering Hebrew and Aramaic medinah (H4082), a jurisdiction or province, from din, to judge, and Greek eparcheia (G1885), a Roman province.
roots_lines: Latin provincia — a territory under a Roman governor, outside Italy.
Hebrew and Aramaic medinah (H4082) — a province, jurisdiction; from din, to judge — a province is defined by whose court it answers to.
Est 1:1 — a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia; the administrative reach that makes Haman's decree irrevocable.
Greek eparcheia (G1885) — a Roman province; the governor's question at Act 23:34 is a jurisdictional one.
Greek hegemon (G2232) — governor; the title of Pilate, Felix, and Festus, the provincial officers of the Gospels and Acts.
usage: “An hundred and seven and twenty provinces” — a decree no ordinary means could stop.
“Over the affairs of the province of Babylon” — believers administering a pagan empire.
“He asked of what province he was” — the jurisdictional question that reached Caesar.

pos: n. (human speech; the words of a nation — in Scripture divided in judgment at Babel and reunited in mercy at Pentecost)
etymology: From Old French langage, from Latin lingua, the tongue. Hebrew does the same thing, using saphah, lip, and lashon, tongue, for a language — the organ standing for what it produces.
biblical_def: The Bible's account of language is a single arc with three points. It begins in unity: “the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech” (Gen 11:1). It is divided in judgment at Babel, where the builders' project of a name and a tower is stopped by a divine act on speech itself: “let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech” (Gen 11:7) — God does not knock the tower down; He makes cooperation impossible. It is reversed in mercy at Pentecost, where the sign is not a restored single tongue but the gospel heard in every existing one: “the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6). The very word Luke uses for the crowd's bewilderment echoes the confounding at Babel. And Zephaniah promises the final resolution: “then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent” (Zep 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines language as human speech; the expression of ideas by words or significant articulate sounds — and also the speech or expression peculiar to a nation.
webster_full: LANGUAGE, n. Human speech; the expression of ideas by words or significant articulate sounds, for the communication of thoughts.
2. Words duly arranged in sentences, written, printed or engraved, and exhibited to the eye.
3. The speech or expression of ideas peculiar to a particular nation.
4. Style; manner of expression.
Note. From the Latin lingua, the tongue, the instrument of speech.
scriptures: Gen 11:1
And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.
Gen 11:7
Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech.
Act 2:6
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
Zep 3:9
For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent.
corruption_summary: Babel is reduced to a folk etymology explaining linguistic diversity, and the gift at Pentecost is detached from the languages it was given in.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as an aetiological myth, Genesis 11 becomes an ancient guess at why people speak differently. Read as Moses wrote it, it is an account of a specific judgment on a specific rebellion: a united humanity building to make itself a name, lest they be scattered — which was precisely what God had commanded them not to avoid (Gen 9:1). The confusion of tongues is not a curse on diversity but a mercy that limits concentrated human rebellion, and the modern impulse toward a single global order administered from one centre would do well to read the chapter as a warning rather than as an origin story.

Pentecost is misread in the other direction whenever the tongues of Acts 2 are separated from actual languages. Luke is explicit and repetitive: every man heard them speak in his own language, and he then lists fifteen regions to make sure the reader cannot mistake him. The sign is that the curse of Babel is being reversed not by erasing the nations but by carrying the gospel into every one of them — which is why Revelation's picture of the redeemed is of every kindred, tongue, people and nation standing together before the throne. Zephaniah's pure language is the same promise: not one tongue restored, but every tongue purified to call upon one name.
roots_summary: Latin lingua, tongue; rendering Hebrew saphah (H8193), lip, and lashon (H3956), tongue, and Greek dialektos (G1258), a dialect or native speech, and glossa (G1100), tongue.
roots_lines: Hebrew saphah (H8193) — lip; “one language” in Gen 11:1 is literally one lip.
Hebrew lashon (H3956) — tongue; the other Hebrew word for a language, and the one behind “every tongue shall confess”.
Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mix, confound; the verb of Gen 11:7 and the wordplay behind the name Babel.
Greek dialektos (G1258) — native speech, dialect; Luke's word at Act 2:6, 8, insisting on real languages.
Greek sugcheo (G4797) — to confound, pour together; used of the crowd at Act 2:6, the Septuagint's verb at Babel.
usage: “The whole earth was of one language” — the unity that preceded the tower.
“There confound their language” — God stops the project by stopping cooperation.
“Every man heard them speak in his own language” — Babel reversed without erasing the nations.

pos: a. (direct, not crooked; in Scripture the condition of the way prepared for the LORD, and of the path a man makes for his own feet)
etymology: From Middle English streight, the past participle of strecchen, to stretch — a straight line is a stretched one. It is a different word from strait, meaning narrow, which comes from Latin strictus; the Authorized Version distinguishes them, and the strait gate of Mat 7:13 is the narrow one, not the straight one.
biblical_def: Straight is the condition of a road fit for a king, and John the Baptist's whole ministry is described by it. Isaiah gives the commission: “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God” (Isa 40:3), which all four Gospels apply to John (Mat 3:3). The image is of an eastern road party going ahead of a monarch, filling valleys and levelling ridges — and what John actually did was preach repentance, which is the levelling. Hebrews puts the same duty on every believer, and adds a pastoral reason: “make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed” (Heb 12:13) — a man's crooked walking trips the weaker Christians behind him. The Preacher marks the limit of human effort: “That which is crooked cannot be made straight” (Ecc 1:15). And the word survives as a street name in the oldest Christian narrative outside the Gospels: “go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth” (Act 9:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines straight as right, in a right line, not crooked; and notes that it is distinct from strait, which signifies narrow, though the two are often confounded.
webster_full: STRAIGHT, a. Right, in a mathematical sense; direct; passing from one point to another by the nearest course.
A straight line is the shortest distance between two points.
2. Narrow; close; tight. [But in this sense strait is now used.]
3. Upright; according with justice and rectitude; not deviating from truth or fairness.
Note. Straight is from stretch; strait, from the Latin strictus, narrow. The words are often confounded.
scriptures: Isa 40:3
The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
Mat 3:3
For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
And make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed.
Ecc 1:15
That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
corruption_summary: “Prepare ye the way” is turned into a slogan for worship atmospherics and revival technique, when John's way of preparing it was to preach repentance and to name particular sins.
corruption_paragraphs: Isa 40:3 is regularly invoked to describe stirring a congregation into a receptive frame, or to justify whatever a ministry proposes as preparation for God's moving. The Gospels leave no doubt what preparation looked like when the man commissioned to do it actually did it: John preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, told the multitude to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, told the publicans to exact no more than was appointed, told the soldiers to do violence to no man and be content with their wages, and told Herod that it was not lawful to have his brother's wife. That last sentence cost him his head. Making the way straight is specific and it is costly.

Ecc 1:15 supplies the limit that keeps the doctrine honest. What is crooked cannot be made straight — not by the man himself. The Preacher is surveying human effort under the sun and finding it unable to correct what is bent, which is exactly the conclusion Romans reaches about the law and the flesh. The straightening in Isaiah is done for God's coming, not by the traveller's own strength, and the levelling John preached was a call to admit crookedness rather than to repair it. Heb 12:13 then gives the believer his actual assignment, which is smaller and more practical: walk straight, because the lame are behind you.
roots_summary: Middle English streight, stretched; rendering Hebrew yashar (H3474), to be straight or upright, and Greek euthus (G2117), straight, and orthos (G3717), upright.
roots_lines: Middle English streight — past participle of strecchen, to stretch; a straight line is a stretched one.
Hebrew yashar (H3474) — to be straight, level, upright; the same root gives Jeshurun, the upright one, a poetic name for Israel.
Greek euthus (G2117) — straight, direct; “make his paths straight” (Mat 3:3), and the adverb eutheos, straightway.
Greek orthos (G3717) — upright, straight; “make straight paths for your feet” (Heb 12:13), whence English orthodox and orthopaedic.
Distinguish strait — Latin strictus, narrow; the strait gate of Mat 7:13 is narrow, not straight, and the KJV keeps the two words apart.
usage: “Make straight in the desert a highway” — and the levelling was preached repentance.
“Make straight paths for your feet” — because the lame are walking behind you.
“That which is crooked cannot be made straight” — not by the man himself.
